title: Rest Is Where the Leaks Cancel

scenes.tts: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at minus seventy-one millivolts. Potassium current leaves it all the time, about two hundred picoamperes. Sodium current enters it all the time, also about two hundred picoamperes. Neither ion is at equilibrium. Yet the voltage does not move. Why?
scenes.caption: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at −71 mV. Potassium current leaves it all the time, about 200 pA. Sodium current enters it all the time, also about 200 pA. Neither ion is at equilibrium. Yet the voltage does not move. Why?
scenes.visual: A neuron cell with a K+ arrow out and a Na+ arrow in, both about 200 pA; a flat Vm trace; a big Why.
scenes.narration: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at −71 mV. Potassium current leaves it all the time, about 200 pA. Sodium current enters it all the time, also about 200 pA. Neither ion is at equilibrium. Yet the voltage does not move. Why?

scenes.tts: Each ion has an equilibrium potential. That is the voltage where the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient. Here the values are supplied. For potassium, E K is minus ninety-five millivolts. For sodium, E N a is plus sixty point six. Driving force is the distance from equilibrium. For potassium it is plus twenty-three point eight millivolts, so the current goes outward. For sodium it is minus one hundred thirty-one point eight, so the current goes inward.

scenes.narration: Each ion has an equilibrium potential. That is the voltage where the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient. Here the values are supplied. For potassium, EK is −95 mV. For sodium, ENa is +60.6 mV. Driving force is the distance from equilibrium. For potassium it is +23.8 mV, so the current goes outward. scenes.tts: Current is conductance times driving force. Potassium has eight point four seven nanosiemens of open leak channels. That gives about two hundred and two picoamperes, outward. Sodium has only one point five three nanosiemens. But its driving force is much larger. It gives two hundred and two picoamperes, inward. The two cancel. Rest means zero net current, not zero current for each ion.
scenes.caption: Current is conductance times driving force. Potassium has 8.47 nS of open leak channels. That gives about +202 pA, outward. Sodium has only 1.53 nS. But its driving force is much larger. It gives −202 pA, inward. The two cancel. Rest means zero net current, not zero current for each ion.
scenes.visual: Two rows, g times driving force equals current, then two equal and opposite bars that cancel to a green net zero.
scenes.narration: Current is conductance times driving force. Potassium has 8.47 nS of open leak channels. That gives about +202 pA, outward. Sodium has only 1.53 nS. But its driving force is much larger. It gives −202 pA, inward. The two cancel. Rest means zero net current, not zero current for each ion.

scenes.tts: Left alone, these leaks would run the gradients down. The sodium potassium pump puts the ions back, three sodium out and two potassium in. Its main job is keeping the gradients. So rest is a steady state held up by the pump. It is not an equilibrium.

scenes.tts: The Goldman Hodgkin Katz equation finds the voltage where total current is zero. Each ion counts in proportion to its relative permeability. In this made-up neuron, potassium is one and sodium is zero point zero four. The result is minus seventy-one point two millivolts. That sits twenty-four millivolts positive of E K. The small sodium leak holds it there.
scenes.caption: The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation finds the voltage where total current is zero. Each ion counts in proportion to its relative permeability. In this made-up neuron, potassium is 1 and sodium is 0.04. The result is −71.2 mV. That sits 24 mV positive of EK. The small sodium leak holds it there.
scenes.visual: Voltage axis with EK and ENa; two permeability bars, PK tall and PNa a sliver; Vm lands near EK with a 24 mV bracket.
scenes.narration: The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation finds the voltage where total current is zero. Each ion counts in proportion to its relative permeability. In this made-up neuron, potassium is 1 and sodium is 0.04. The result is −71.2 mV. That sits 24 mV positive of EK. The small sodium leak holds it there.

scenes.tts: Now double the sodium permeability, to zero point zero eight. The balance point moves to minus fifty-eight point nine millivolts. That is twelve millivolts toward E N a. Raising one ion's permeability moves the voltage toward that ion's equilibrium potential. Other cells have other ratios, so there is no universal resting potential. Keep this rule. Rest is where the leaks cancel, and permeability sets where.
scenes.caption: Now double the sodium permeability, to 0.08. The balance point moves to −58.9 mV. That is 12 mV toward ENa. Rest is where the leaks cancel, and permeability sets where.
